explanation:
## The loop

```cpp
for (int i = 1; i <= n; ++i)
{
    bool by3{ i % 3 == 0 };
    bool by5{ i % 5 == 0 };

    if (by3 && by5)   std::cout << "both\n";
    else if (by3)     std::cout << "three\n";
    else if (by5)     std::cout << "five\n";
    else              std::cout << i << "\n";
}
```

## The three parts of a for

```
for ( init ; condition ; update )
      ^       ^           ^
      runs    tested      runs after
      once    before      each pass
      first   each pass
```

So `for (int i = 1; i <= n; ++i)` starts at 1, keeps going while `i` is at most
`n`, and adds one each time round. The condition is tested **before** the first
pass, which is why `n = 0` prints nothing with no special case: `1 <= 0` is
false and the body never runs.

That is worth noticing. A `for` whose range is empty is not an error to guard
against; it is the loop working correctly on no items. Writing `if (n > 0)`
around it would be noise.

**`<=` not `<`.** The range includes `n`, so the test is `i <= n`. With `<` the
loop stops one short and `n = 7` prints only six lines. Off-by-one in a loop
bound is the single most common loop bug, and the fix is to decide *before*
writing it whether the last value is included.

**Declare `i` in the header.** `for (int i = ...)` scopes `i` to the loop, so it
cannot be read afterwards by accident and the name is free for the next loop.
Declaring it above the loop is a C habit and leaks the variable.

## Why `both` has to be tested first

15 divides by 3 *and* by 5. Both `by3` and `by5` are true, so whichever
single-divisor test comes first will claim it:

```cpp
if (by3)            std::cout << "three\n";   // 15 lands here
else if (by5)       std::cout << "five\n";
else if (by3 && by5) std::cout << "both\n";   // unreachable, always
```

The most specific case goes first. This is the same rule as the bands problem,
and it generalises: **in an else-if chain, order from narrowest to widest.**

## `%` and negative numbers

`i % 3` is a remainder, and it is zero exactly when 3 divides `i`. The loop here
only ever sees positive `i`, which is worth knowing because C++ `%` on a
negative left operand gives a **negative** remainder: `-7 % 3` is `-1`, not `2`.
So `x % 3 == 0` is still a correct divisibility test for negatives, but
`x % 3 == 1` is not what you would expect. Not a problem here; a real one the
first time you write a hash function.

## Two bools instead of four comparisons

Computing `by3` and `by5` once and naming them is shorter, says what the
condition *means* rather than how it is computed, and makes `by3 && by5` read as
the English sentence it is. The compiler generates the same code either way, so
this is purely about the reader — which is the only thing it needs to be about.
